newsitem.title: UK: N Sea, Urals hold firm on Iraq news.
newsitem.headline: N Sea, Urals hold firm on Iraq news.

text.p: Sweet North Sea crude oil grades look set to hold last week's firmer levels and may see further gains after a rush of buying on Friday saw over seven million barrels of the July loading programme change hands, traders said.
Urals held firm with little on offer though traders said they were not surprised by weekend news that Iraq did not expect to resume loadings until August.

On Saturday, Iraq's key negotiator for a U.N. oil-for-food deal said that Baghdad was ready to resume new oil sales in August under the second round of the accord approved this month if New York did not delay agreement.

Abdul Amir al-Anbari told Reuters that Baghdad was ready to resume crude shipments pending submission of its medicine and food distribution plan, likely to be ready within two weeks, and Security Council approval.
"Everything is really in place. It depends on how cooperative the other party is," said the envoy.
If all went smoothly, al-Anbari said: "End of July, beginning of August we would resume our oil discussions. We'll have to sign contracts and they have to be approved by the oil experts in New York."

As outright prices gained ground on Monday intermonth spreads followed suit. August Brent on the IPE was trading up 17 cents at $18.35 a barrel by 1042 GMT. The Jul/Aug Brent traded at -11 cents but was later bid at -10 cents with best offer two cents firmer.

There were no Brent cargoes due to turn wet on Monday from the original loading schedule and traders said they had not heard of any being brought forward. Only one (July 16-18) cargo was due to turn wet on Tuesday.
One of the cargoes (July 14-16) kept before the five o'clock deadline on Friday was heard later sold to an end-user at July Brent -1 cent.

"This market is strong and possibly getting stronger in the short term. I can't see anything getting cheaper following the news about Iraq. There isn't much North Sea crude left (in July," one European refiner said.
In the Mediterranean traders reacted calmly to news of further delays to Iraqi exports, saying the market had already doubted the early July target date given last week by Iraq's oil minister.
"It doesn't surprise me, nobody really believed the target anyway," said one buyer of Russian Urals, the alternative Mediterranean sour crude.
"For July it's a Urals market only and basically people are short, the situation is tight," he added.

A Spanish refiner was heard to have bought fob Urals barrels last Thursday for a price equivalent to around 70 cents a barrel below dated Brent. With little on offer, the price was nominally the same on Monday.

Some West African barrels were already believed en route to the Med for July but would provide little relief. Only poor refinery margins, pressuring refiners to cut their purchases, would ease the situation, one trader said.
